extracted.intended_audience: The People of the State of New York; citizens considering ratification of the proposed Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political-essay arguments defending a strong federal authority over national defense, military establishments, and related fiscal powers in the proposed U.S. Constitution. The text assesses the proper allocation of powers between federal and state governments and critiques restraints on legislative discretion over military matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal power to levy and support forces
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union ought to be invested with full power to levy troops; to build and equip fleets; and to raise the revenues which will be required for the formation and support of an army and navy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These powers should be vested in the national government in the customary and ordinary modes practiced in other governments; they are necessary to manage national interests and common defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of powers by object (discrimination of objects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discriminate the OBJECTS which shall appertain to the different provinces or departments of power; allowing to each the most ample authority for fulfilling the objects committed to its charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each government (federal or state) must be given powers commensurate to its assigned ends; failing to confer adequate authority frustrates prudent administration and proper management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal guardianship of common safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union should be constituted the guardian of the common safety, empowered to pass all laws and make all regulations which have relation to fleets, armies, revenues, commerce, and other matters within its jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the federal body is the centre of information, representative of the whole, and can establish uniformity and concert, it is best suited to make provisions for public defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility for internal justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The administration of justice between the citizens of the same State is the proper department of the local governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local governments must possess the authorities connected with administering local civil justice and other matters allotted to their cognizance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers must be commensurate to national interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever NATIONAL INTERESTS can with propriety be confided, the coincident powers may safely accompany them; the POWERS are not too extensive for the OBJECTS of federal administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents should show that the internal structure renders the proposed government unworthy of confidence rather than merely declaim about extent; powers should align with the objects they manage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization to ensure cooperation and uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Devolving care of common defense to State governments under direction of the Union would transfer the federal head's care to individual members, producing inconsistency, lack of co-operation, weakness, disorder, unequal burdens, and increased expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because dangers and territories are common across states, means of guarding against them ought to be objects of common councils and a common treasury; separate provisions risk rivalry and strategic imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative (not executive) authority to raise armies
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole power of raising armies is lodged in the LEGISLATURE, not in the EXECUTIVE; the legislature is a popular body of periodically elected representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing the power in the legislature provides accountability and is preferable to vesting it in the executive; legislative appropriations and periodic elections are checks on misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial appropriation as a check on standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause forbidding the appropriation of money for the support of an army for any longer period than two years is an important qualification and a real security against keeping up troops without evident necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting appropriations to two-year terms constrains permanent standing armies while leaving the legislature discretion to respond to need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on legislative discretion regarding military establishments are improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraints upon the discretion of the legislature in respect to military establishments in time of peace would be improper to be imposed, and if imposed, from the necessities of society, would be unlikely to be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because exigencies arise that require military action or maintenance in peace, constitutionally fettering the legislature is impracticable and dangerous to public safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition against raising armies in peace is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: If prohibition extended to the RAISING of armies in time of peace, the United States would be incapacitated by its Constitution to prepare for defense before being actually invaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nation must be able to anticipate and prepare for danger; forbidding raising armies precludes preemptive defense and invites invasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness of prohibitions undermines effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions that forbid 'keeping up' armies without defining duration or conditions (week, month, year, or while danger continues) will be ineffectual and subject to broad construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional language must avoid vague terms that leave crucial judgments (like continuance of danger) to those whose interests may exploit the ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia alone is insufficient for sustained warfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The militia, though valiant, cannot alone sustain the steady operations of war against a regular and disciplined army; war is a science requiring diligence, perseverance, time, and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience from the Revolution shows reliance on militia alone nearly lost independence; economy and stability also favor a regular force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical necessity trumps formal prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: States with constitutional cautions against standing armies have nonetheless raised and maintained troops in peace when necessity required—demonstrating that parchment provisions are unequal to public necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Pennsylvania, Massachusetts) show that practical needs will lead governments to act despite prohibitions; hence unconstitutional fetters are unlikely to be honored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dual possession of military forces by states
rubrics_metrics.description: If individual States possess separate military forces, mutual jealousy and rivalry would enlarge those establishments and create engines for abridging or demolishing national authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National forces should be in national hands to prevent states from becoming militarily independent powers and threatening the Union or balance among states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geopolitical realities require preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proximity of British and Spanish territories, susceptible Indian tribes, and improvements in navigation make distant powers effectively neighbors; these circumstances admonish against excessive confidence and require readiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given likely foreign alignments and frontier threats, the nation must be able to provide garrisons, a navy, dockyards, arsenals, and fortifications as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frontier defense requires permanent garrisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Small garrisons on the Western frontier are indispensable; militia detachments are impracticable and would burden citizens; permanent corps in government pay constitute a standing army but are required for security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia would not long submit to repeated service; rotation of militia is costly and disruptive, so some permanent forces are necessary for frontier posts and key territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval defense demands infrastructure and garrisons
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a commercial people secure on the Atlantic side, we must have a navy, dock-yards and arsenals; while naval power is immature, fortifications and moderate garrisons are necessary to protect those establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naval infancy implies temporary dependence on shore fortifications and garrisons until fleets can fully secure naval infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unenforceable restrictions erode constitutional reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fettering government with restrictions that cannot be observed impairs the sacred reverence for the constitution and forms precedent for other breaches when necessity later arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should avoid imposing impracticable restraints that the government will breach out of necessity, thereby undermining long-term constitutional stability.
